lmsArticle.title: Top K Elements Pattern: Find the Best K Without Sorting Everything
lmsArticle.subtitle: Maintain a min-heap of size K. Anything smaller than the current minimum gets evicted immediately.
lmsArticle.excerpt: To find the top K largest elements, maintain a **min-heap of size K**. For every new element, push it onto the heap. If the heap exceeds K, evict the minimum. After processing all N elements, the heap holds exactly the K largest. O(N log K) time — orders of magnitude faster than sorting when K is small.
lmsArticle.content:
## Scenario context

To find the top K largest elements, maintain a **min-heap of size K**. For every new element, push it onto the heap. If the heap exceeds K, evict the minimum. After processing all N elements, the heap holds exactly the K largest. O(N log K) time — orders of magnitude faster than sorting when K is small.

---

Twitter needs to show the top 10 trending hashtags from 50 million tweets in real time. Sorting all 50 milli…

This walkthrough focuses on **The 50-Million-Tweet Problem: Why You Cannot Sort Everything**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- Twitter needs to show the top 10 trending hashtags from 50 million tweets in real time.
- Sorting all 50 million records to find the top 10 would take O(N log N) — roughly 50M × 25 = 1.25 billion operations.
- For a system processing new tweets every millisecond, this is unacceptable.

**Concepts in play:** tree-data-structures, jvm-internals-and-garbage-collection, database-indexing, core-algorithm-patterns

## Stage 1 — Min-Heap of Size K: The Eviction Strategy That Finds the Top K

- The strategy sounds counterintuitive: to find the K largest elements, you use a min-heap .
- A min-heap of size K holds the K largest elements seen so far.
- Its root is the smallest of those K elements — the weakest member of your current top-K leaderboard.
- When a new element arrives: - If it is larger than the root , it can displace the weakest champion.

*Applies **tree-data-structures** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** When a new element arrives: - If it is larger than the root , it can displace the weakest champion.

## Stage 2 — Min-Heap for Top K Largest, Max-Heap for Top K Smallest

- The core algorithm in three lines of logic: After the loop, heap holds the answer.
- Worked example — top 3 largest from [3, 1, 5, 12, 2, 11, 7]: Result: top 3 largest = {7, 11, 12}.
- The heap never grew beyond K = 3.
- In Java: No comparator needed for top-K-largest — the default min-heap is exactly what you want.

*Applies **jvm-internals-and-garbage-collection** to the decision above.*

```
for each element x in the collection:
    heap.offer(x)
    if heap.size() > K:
        heap.poll()   // evict the "weakest" candidate
```

```java
PriorityQueue<Integer> minHeap = new PriorityQueue<>(); // default: min-heap
```

**Observable outcome:** In Java: No comparator needed for top-K-largest — the default min-heap is exactly what you want.

## Stage 3 — Deep Dive: How PriorityQueue Handles K-Bounded Heap Operations

- Internals: Heap Sift-Up, Sift-Down, and the Eviction Trigger Java's PriorityQueue is a binary heap in an array .
- The key invariant: every node is less than or equal to its children.
- The root (index 0) is always the minimum — accessible in O(1) via peek() .
- offer(x) places the new element at the array's tail (index size ) and sifts up : it compares the element to its parent at (i-1)/2 and swaps if necessary, repeating until the heap property is satisfied.

*Applies **database-indexing** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** offer(x) places the new element at the array's tail (index size ) and sifts up : it compares the element to its parent at (i-1)/2 and swaps if necessary, repeating until the heap property is satisfied.

## Stage 4 — Visualizing Heap Eviction as Elements Arrive

- The flowchart below shows the per-element decision loop, including the eviction trigger that keeps the heap bounded at K: After the main loop, draining the heap gives the K elements in ascending order.
- If you need descending order (largest first), drain into an array and reverse, or use Collections.reverseOrder() on a second pass.

*Applies **core-algorithm-patterns** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A([Next element x]) --> B[heap.offer x]
    B --> C{heap.size > K?}
    C -- Yes --> D[heap.poll  evict minimum]
    C -- No --> E{More elements?}
    D --> E
    E -- Yes --> A
    E -- No --> F[heap contains top K elements]
    F --> G{Need K elements in order?}
    G -- Yes --> H[Drain heap into array  O K log K]
    G -- No --> I[Return heap directly]
```

**Observable outcome:** If you need descending order (largest first), drain into an array and reverse, or use Collections.reverseOrder() on a second pass.

## Stage 5 — Real-World Applications: Trending Hashtags, Recommendations, and Monitoring

- Social media trending — Twitter and TikTok compute top-K hashtags or topics from a sliding window of recent activity.
- A frequency map builds the counts; a min-heap of size K runs over the map entries.
- The entire pipeline fits in a single O(N log K) pass, meaning trending can refresh every few seconds even at billions of events per day.
- Recommendation engines — Spotify's "Daily Mix" selects the K most relevant tracks from a catalog of 100 million songs.

*Applies **tree-data-structures** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Recommendation engines — Spotify's "Daily Mix" selects the K most relevant tracks from a catalog of 100 million songs.

## Stage 6 — Java PriorityQueue and Guava's MinMaxPriorityQueue in Practice

- Java's PriorityQueue is the idiomatic choice and sufficient for all four problems above.
- Two limitations worth knowing: 1.
- PriorityQueue is not thread-safe .
- For concurrent stream processing, use java.util.concurrent.PriorityBlockingQueue or externally synchronize.

*Applies **jvm-internals-and-garbage-collection** to the decision above.*

```java
// Guava dependency: com.google.guava:guava
import com.google.common.collect.MinMaxPriorityQueue;

MinMaxPriorityQueue<Integer> deque = MinMaxPriorityQueue
        .maximumSize(k)   // automatically evicts the minimum when size exceeds K
        .create();

deque.add(5);
deque.add(1);
deque.add(10);
// deque.peekLast() = minimum; deque.peekFirst() = maximum
```

**Observable outcome:** For concurrent stream processing, use java.util.concurrent.PriorityBlockingQueue or externally synchronize.

## End-to-end outcome

After working through the stages, you should be able to explain:

- Using the wrong heap direction.
- This is the 1 interview mistake.
- - Core idea: A min-heap of size K acts as a rolling leaderboard — every new element challenges the weakest current champion.
- If it wins, the champion is evicted.

seriesList.name: Architecture Patterns for Production Systems
seriesList.description: High-level design is only half the battle; the other half is surviving production. This series explores the architectural patterns required to build resilient, scalable, and maintainable systems. We dive into the trade-offs of microservices vs. monoliths, event-driven architectures, caching strategies, and data consistency models. Each post focuses on proven patterns that solve common bottlenecks in high-traffic production environments, helping you move from "it works on my machine" to "it works at scale."

seriesList.name: Data Structures and Algorithms
seriesList.description: Master the core of computer science. This series demystifies Data Structures and Algorithms, from Big O to graph theory. Learn to write efficient, scalable code and ace your technical interviews with confidence.

seriesList.name: How It Works: Internals Explained
seriesList.description: Ever wondered what actually happens when you trigger a function, commit a transaction, or deploy a container? This series peels back the layers of abstraction to explore the low-level mechanics of modern technology. From database engines and operating system internals to the hidden plumbing of distributed systems, we dive deep into the source code and architectural designs that make complex software work. No magic, just engineering.

seriesList.name: Low-Level Design Guide
seriesList.description: Good architecture is built on a foundation of solid low-level design. This series is a deep dive into the "micro" side of software engineering—focusing on class design, object-oriented principles (SOLID), and tactical design patterns. We explore how to translate requirements into clean, maintainable code, handle concurrency at the component level, and define clear interfaces. Whether you're preparing for LLD interviews or looking to sharpen your day-to-day coding craftsmanship, this guide provides the blueprints for building modular software.

seriesList.name: Machine Learning Fundamentals
seriesList.description: This series breaks down complex mathematical theories and algorithms into simple, intuitive explanations with practical examples, making AI accessible to everyone from beginners to aspiring data scientists.

seriesList.name: Software Engineering Principles
seriesList.description: Writing code is easy; engineering software that lasts is hard. This series explores the core philosophies and mental models that define professional software development. We go beyond syntax to discuss the timeless principles of modularity, abstraction, testing strategies, and technical debt management. Whether we’re discussing the Zen of Python or the rigors of formal verification, this series provides a high-level perspective on how to think like an engineer, not just a coder.
